pilot.summary: Three-player pod at Tom Beloy's — Alex on mono-red Tannuk, Tom on Merfolk. Alex resolved Blood Moon on turn two or three and every nonbasic became a Mountain, so Smothering Tithe and everything multicoloured were uncastable and I was down to the all-red dragons. I got there with Moltensteel Dragon at the end, paying sixteen life to pump it and hitting Alex for twelve. I am not building around Blood Moon; the lesson I took was to have the mana base audited holistically.

Five-player pod at Oliver's, seat 4, and the first game on the new land base after raising it 31 to 36 that same day. It did not help — mulliganed once, sat on four or five lands on turns six and seven while Alex was tapping for twelve on turns four and five, and the cost reducer got removed so the discount engine never did its job. After that it was repeated wipes: board established, board erased. I won by staying off the radar and closing at the end, and my own read is that the deck did not win, the table's attrition did.

Game 2 of three at Oliver's, five-player pod, and the first validation game for the refactor. The mana worked — turn-one land into Sol Ring and Arcane Signet, turn-two Bloom Tender — and I curved into Miirym, Gadrak and Terror of the Peaks. Then I played Gadrak a turn too early and telegraphed the whole thing: the table read "Sean is swinging for 28 in the air" and converged, Tom killing all three artifacts so Gadrak could not activate, Alex fighting the dragons with his fight deck, Ryan removing more. Loss, and the lesson written down was speed without protection or politics makes me the obvious kill target before I can close.

Four-player pod at my house — Stuart on an Animar precon, Steven on CC Weather, David on Squirrels. I sacked a land to tutor, found Terror of the Peaks, and after that every dragon ETB was about ten targeted damage across three targets, which I used as spot removal to take out two commanders. Then I telegraphed again: the treasure pile plus fireballing every ETB made me the obvious problem, David called it out, and three players picked me apart inside one rotation. Steven flew under the radar with his tap/untap engine and won it — a political loss, not a deck loss.

Five-player pod at Oliver's; I arrived late, missed game one, and Oliver won every game that night. I was going to play Heliod and swapped to Ur-Dragon because the table said "creatures". No green source all game, so Farseek and the green dragons sat in hand, and Enlightened Tutor went for Sol Ring when it should have found a green rock or a signet. Firespitter Whelp with Twinflame Tyrant and Panharmonicon was pinging and doubling, but I cast Twinflame before the big dragons were down and it was removed immediately — the same too-early pattern, no treasure engine online at any point, and no counterspells left to answer any of it.

read.what_it_does: It ramps early, buys the dragons down and turns every arrival into targeted damage. Terror of the Peaks is the card the games keep coming back to: about ten damage spread across three targets on each ETB, used as spot removal, and it killed two commanders in one game (004). That confirms what the manual says the damage leg is, and the games add the part the decklist cannot: the kill it actually presents at a table is ETB burn, not a combat swing, and it has never closed a game by killing the pod — the one win came from sitting quiet while four other players ground each other down (002).
read.how_it_plays: Fast and loud. When the mana cooperates it is the quickest deck at the table by several turns — turn-one Sol Ring and Arcane Signet, turn-two Bloom Tender (003) — and the board it builds is legible from across the table. Sitting behind it, the tells are the treasure pile and the fireball on every ETB (004). What happens next is the same both times: the pod reads lethal in the air before lethal is actually presentable and converges — Tom killing all three artifacts so Gadrak could not activate, Alex fighting the dragons, Ryan removing more (003); three players picking the deck apart inside one rotation (004). Where it ends up is dead to a converged table (003, 004), stalled behind missing colour (005), or, once, last seat standing by being invisible (002).
mindful_of: The board goes down too early, three games running. Gadrak a turn ahead of the payoff (003); every ETB fireballed and the treasure stacked in plain sight (004); Twinflame Tyrant cast before the big dragons were down, and removed immediately (005). Sean named the cause himself in 005 — he does not like having unspent mana. Dropping the tempo a turn or two is the fix he wrote down.

There are no responses. Since the refactor pulled the counterspells there is nothing to protect a dragon or answer the converge, and both recent games say so: "I cut protection and counters for speed, and it showed" (003), "I now have zero responses" (005).

Politics is the recorded cause of two losses (003, 004). In 004 the quiet assembler won it — Steven's tap/untap engine went unanswered while the table was busy with the dragons. The standing lesson is to manage his own optics and to point the table at the quiet seat before it is unanswerable.

Green is the colour that goes missing. No green source at all in 005, with Farseek and the green-needing dragons stranded in hand, even though Delighted Halfling, Birds of Paradise and Bloom Tender are all in the 99. His own proposed rule: no green source, consider shipping the hand.
Tutors get spent on speed instead of on the problem in front of him — Enlightened Tutor found Sol Ring when the game was a fixing game (005).

The pod at Oliver's runs heavy creature removal and board wipes, and this deck makes nothing on the way down: board established, board erased, repeat, with the cost reducer removed so the discount engine never fired (002, on V2). The removal half of that has not changed — 003 and 004 are both the table taking the board apart.
Deck choice can be its own problem. He swapped off Heliod to Ur-Dragon because the table said "creatures" (005), and his own view is that mismatched decks make salt.
Temperament. He wanted to scoop in 005, took a breath and played it out. The rule he set for himself is to stay on the field and get even inside the game.
read.what_changed: Three changes in four versions, and the games price each one differently. V1 was 31 lands; after the Blood Moon game (001) the ask was a holistic mana audit, and V2 raised the count to 36 the same week. It did not show up: the first game on the new base was still four or five lands on turns six and seven while the table was on eight to ten plus dorks (002). V3 — the eminence-v3 merge — swapped density toward dorks and rocks, and that one did land: "The mana worked" (003). The same merge pulled every counterspell — Counterspell, Dovin's Veto, Swan Song — and the deck has had zero responses since, which is the one change that shows up in every game after it (003, 005). It also cut Smothering Tithe and Moltensteel Dragon, so the card-level half of 001 is superseded: that was true of a list this deck no longer runs, and only its mana-base finding still applies. V4 was two proxy duals becoming budget lands; nothing in the last two games turns on those two cards, and the mana failure in 005 was colour, not count.
